messages.content:
You are an expert power-electronics designer synthesising the interface circuit of a
piezoelectric energy harvester. You work by experiment: you propose a circuit, it is simulated in
LTspice under several operating conditions, and you receive the measurements.

GOAL
A piezo transducer must power a sensor-node load RL from a storage capacitor at node "out".
Under EVERY operating condition below, starting from 0 V (cold start) and simulating 0.8 s:
  vout_min: vavg >= 1.8 V (settled mean output reaches the load's minimum supply)
  vout_max: vmax <= 3.6 V (output never exceeds the load's absolute maximum)
  ripple: vpp <= 0.05 V (peak-to-peak ripple in the final window)
  startup: tup <= 0.4 s (cold start: first time output reaches 1.8 V)
  settled: dv <= 0.02 V (mean output changes little between the last two windows)
Measurement windows: vavg and vpp over 0.7-0.8 s; vmax over the whole run; tup = first time
V(out) reaches 1.8 V (missing if never); dv = |mean(0.7-0.8 s) - mean(0.6-0.7 s)|.

PIEZO MODEL AND OPERATING CONDITIONS
The piezo is a sinusoidal current source Ip*sin(2*pi*f*t) in parallel with its capacitance Cp and a
20 MOhm leakage resistance, between nodes pzp and pzn (Cp = 25 nF nominal).
Its open-circuit voltage amplitude is Ip/(2*pi*f*Cp), about 3.2 V at nominal: low, so diode drops matter.
  S1: nominal; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 330 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S2: heavy load; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 150 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S3: strong excitation, light load; Ip = 100 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 2200 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S4: weak excitation; Ip = 30 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 1000 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S5: low frequency; Ip = 40 uA peak, f = 80 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 470 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S6: Cp +20 %, hot; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 30 nF, RL = 330 kOhm, temperature 60 C

TEST BENCH (fixed, added automatically - do not include these)
- the piezo model between pzp and pzn; the load RL from out to 0;
- for every SYNC controller you use, a 0.5 uA supply current drawn from out (its power cost);
- a 1 GOhm resistor to 0 from pzp, pzn and every internal node (prevents floating nodes).

COMPONENTS YOU MAY USE (at most 16 components)
- R  resistor, value 1..1e+08 Ohm, nodes [a, b]
- C  capacitor, value 1e-10..4.7e-05 F, nodes [a, b]
- L  inductor, value 1e-05..0.01 H; it has series resistance 2 Ohm + 5 Ohm per mH
- D  diode, nodes [anode, cathode]: forward current flows from the first node to the second.
     Model one of DSCH, DSI, DZ33:
     DSCH = low-drop Schottky (~0.25 V at uA), DSI = silicon small-signal (~0.5 V at uA),
     DZ33 = 3.3 V zener (reverse breakdown 3.3 V, conducts ~1 uA at 3.3 V and much more above)
     Orientation matters:
       full bridge: ["pzp", "out"], ["pzn", "out"], ["0", "pzp"], ["0", "pzn"] (return diodes have
       their anode on ground);
       zener clamp on out: ["0", "out"] (cathode on out, so it is reverse-biased and breaks down at
       3.3 V). ["out", "0"] would be forward-biased and hold out near 0.7 V; it is rejected.
- S  switch, nodes [a, b], "ctrl": id of a SYNC; Ron = 2 Ohm, Roff = 1 GOhm (at most 4)
- SYNC ideal synchronous controller (no nodes, at most 2): closes its switches for "ton"
     seconds (1e-07..0.001) at the piezo voltage extrema, which occur at the zero
     crossings of the piezo current. "edges": "both" (every half period), "pos" (positive peak only)
     or "neg" (negative peak only). "phase" shifts the pulses by that fraction of the excitation
     period (-0.25..0.25). It tracks the excitation frequency automatically.
     For L-Cp inversion, ton is about pi*sqrt(L*Cp).
Nodes: "0" is ground; pzp, pzn are the piezo terminals; out is the load/storage node; name any other
nodes yourself (lower-case, e.g. n1, mid). Every node needs at least two connections, and out must
connect to the piezo through your circuit.

REFERENCE DESIGN: FBR (full-bridge rectifier, 4 x DSCH, 2.2 uF on out). Its results:
cond   vavg V  vmax V  vpp mV   tup s  Pload uW  vout_min vout_max ripple   startup  settled 
S1       2.24    2.25    26.2   0.269      15.2  ok       ok       ok       ok       FAIL    
S2       1.76    1.77    20.3       -      20.7  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     ok      
S3       5.68    5.72    84.4  0.0779      14.7  ok       FAIL     FAIL     ok       FAIL    
S4       1.51    1.52    20.8       -      2.27  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     FAIL    
S5       2.26    2.28    43.5   0.318      10.9  ok       ok       ok       ok       FAIL    
S6       1.93    1.94    18.8   0.379      11.3  ok       ok       ok       ok       ok      

HOW TO WORK
- Component values are optimised automatically (an evolution strategy, up to 48 full
  evaluations per structure, running while you think), so spend your reasoning on circuit
  CONNECTIVITY (topology): which structure can meet every condition. A structure that was already
  explored is not simulated again, whatever its values.
- Each round, propose up to 3 designs with DIFFERENT connectivity (different structures, not value variants).
- Classify each design with "move": new_topology or modify_topology, and explain the expected effect
  in "rationale". Set "done": true only when you believe no further structural change can improve on
  the best design so far.
- Reply with ONE JSON object only, in this form:
{
 "proposals": [
  {
   "move": "new_topology",
   "name": "short label for this design",
   "rationale": "what you changed and why it should fix the failing checks",
   "done": false,
   "components": [
    {
     "id": "D1",
     "type": "D",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "out"
     ],
     "model": "DSCH"
    },
    {
     "id": "C1",
     "type": "C",
     "nodes": [
      "out",
      "0"
     ],
     "value": 2.2e-06
    },
    {
     "id": "L1",
     "type": "L",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "n1"
     ],
     "value": 0.0047
    },
    {
     "id": "S1",
     "type": "S",
     "nodes": [
      "n1",
      "pzn"
     ],
     "ctrl": "G1"
    },
    {
     "id": "G1",
     "type": "SYNC",
     "ton": 3.4e-05,
     "phase": 0.0,
     "edges": "both"
    }
   ]
  }
 ]
}

Round 1 of 12.

This is your first round: choose the structures you think most likely to meet every condition.

Reply with one JSON object only.

reply.reasoning:
*   Input: Piezo transducer (sinusoidal current source, Cp = 25nF, R_leak = 20MOhm).
    *   Output: Storage capacitor at node `out` powering load $R_L$.
    *   Goal:
        *   $V_{avg} \ge 1.8\text{V}$
        *   $V_{max} \le 3.6\text{V}$
        *   $V_{pp} \le 0.05\text{V}$
        *   $t_{up} \le 0.4\text{s}$
        *   $dV \le 0.02\text{V}$
    *   Challenges:
        *   Low open-circuit voltage ($V_{oc} \approx 3.2\text{V}$), so diode drops are significant.
        *   Varying loads ($150\text{k}\Omega$ to $2.2\text{M}\Omega$).
        *   Varying excitations (Ip = 30uA to 100uA).
        *   $V_{max}$ constraint is tight (3.6V).

    *   FBR (Full-Bridge Rectifier) fails because:
        *   S2 (heavy load): $V_{avg} < 1.8\text{V}$ (too much load, diode drops).
        *   S3 (light load, strong excitation): $V_{max} > 3.6\text{V}$ (overvoltage).
        *   S4 (weak excitation): $V_{avg} < 1.8\text{V}$ (not enough power, diode drops).
        *   S5: $dV$ failure (stability).

    *   *Standard Bridge Rectifier*: Simple but high drop (2 diodes).
    *   *Synchronous Rectification (SSHI or similar)*: Uses switches to reduce losses and potentially increase voltage.
    *   *Synchronous Electric Charge Extraction (SECE)*: Extracts charge at the peaks of the piezo voltage.
    *   *Zener Clamp*: To prevent $V_{max} > 3.6\text{V}$.
    *   *Active Rectification/Synchronous Switch Harvesting (SSHI)*: To invert the voltage on $C_p$ at the peaks, effectively multiplying the harvested energy.

    *   **Proposal 1: Bridge Rectifier + Zener Clamp**
        *   This is the FBR plus a DZ33 zener to protect from S3 overvoltage.
        *   However, FBR still fails S2 and S4 due to diode drops.

    *   **Proposal 2: Synchronous Switch Harvesting on Inductor (SSHI - simplified)**
        *   Use an inductor $L$ and a switch $S$ to flip the voltage on $C_p$ at the peaks.
        *   Then rectify that flipped voltage into the storage capacitor.
        *   Wait, a simple SSHI uses a switch to flip $C_p$ and then a rectifier.
        *   Let's try a "Parallel-SSHI" or a "Buck-converter-like" structure if possible, but the constraints on components are tight.
        *   Actually, a simpler way to reduce diode drops is a half-wave rectifier with a synchronous switch (Synchronous Electric Charge Extraction - SECE) or a synchronized switch to move charge to the storage capacitor.

    *   **Proposal 3: SECE-like (Synchronous Electric Charge Extraction)**
        *   Use a switch and an inductor to transfer the charge from $C_p$ to $C_{out}$ at the peaks.
        *   At the voltage peaks (where current is zero), the switch closes, and the energy in $C_p$ is transferred to $C_{out}$ through $L$.
        *   Wait, SECE usually requires a specific timing. The `SYNC` controller closes switches at extrema.
        *   Topology: $C_p$ is part of the piezo. An inductor $L$ connects from $pzp$ to $out$ (or via a switch).
        *   Let's refine: A switch between $pzp$ and $L$, then $L$ to $out$. If the switch closes at the peak of $V_{pzp}$, energy flows into $C_{out}$. But we need to avoid backflow. A diode is needed.

    *   **Proposal 4: Improved Bridge (Symmetric Synchronous Rectifier)**
        *   Replace the diodes of the bridge with switches. But we only have 4 switches.
        *   A full bridge has 4 diodes. We could use switches to replace some.

    *   **Proposal 5: The "Inductor-First" Boost/Inversion (SSHI)**
        *   Inductor $L$ and Switch $S$ in parallel with the piezo (between $pzp$ and $pzn$).
        *   When $S$ closes at the peak of $V_{pzp}$, the energy in $C_p$ is flipped.
        *   This increases the effective $V_{oc}$. Then a bridge rectifier feeds $C_{out}$.
        *   This requires 4 diodes + 1 switch + 1 inductor.

    *   *S2 (Heavy Load)* and *S4 (Weak Excitation)* are the hardest. They both fail $V_{avg} \ge 1.8\text{V}$. This means we need higher efficiency (lower drops) and/or higher voltage.
    *   The FBR has 2 diode drops (approx $0.25\text{V} \times 2 = 0.5\text{V}$). $V_{oc}$ is $3.2\text{V}$.
    *   A Synchronous Switch (SSHI) can increase the voltage harvested from $C_p$.

    *   *Topology 1: SSHI + FBR*
        *   $L1$ and $S1$ in parallel with piezo (pzp to pzn).
        *   FBR (D1-D4) from pzp, pzn to out.
        *   Cout on out.
        *   Zener DZ33 on out.
        *   This should increase the voltage available to the rectifier.

    *   *Topology 2: SECE (Simplified)*
        *   $pzp \to S1 \to L1 \to D1 \to out$.
        *   $pzn \to S2 \to L2 \to D2 \to out$.
        *   (But we only have 4 switches total, and 2 SYNCs).
        *   Actually, $S1$ closes at positive peak, $S2$ at negative peak.
        *   Wait, the SYNC controller can do `edges: both`.
        *   Let's try: $pzp \to L1 \to S1 \to out$. No, that doesn't work.
        *   Let's try: $pzp \to S1 \to n1$, $n1 \to L1 \to out$, $S1$ closes at peak. This is a charge pump.

    *   *Topology 3: Half-bridge / Charge Pump*
        *   Use the SYNC to create a buck-boost effect.

    *   *Let's revisit the FBR failure.*
        *   S2: $V_{avg} = 1.76\text{V}$ (close!).
        *   S4: $V_{avg} = 1.51\text{V}$ (needs a boost).
        *   S3: $V_{max} = 5.72\text{V}$ (needs a clamp).

    *   If I add a Zener to FBR, S3 is solved. To solve S2 and S4, I need more voltage.
    *   SSHI (Synchronous Switch Harvesting on Inductor) is the classic way to do this.
    *   SSHI basic: Inductor $L$ and switch $S$ are in parallel with the piezo. The switch closes at the voltage peak, causing an LC oscillation that flips the voltage on $C_p$.
    *   Wait, if I put $L$ and $S$ in parallel with the piezo, the bridge rectifier still has 2 diode drops.

    *   Is there a way to get a *lower* voltage drop than a bridge?
    *   A half-bridge? No, that wastes half the energy.
    *   A synchronous rectifier (replacing diodes with switches)?
    *   If I use switches for the bridge:
        *   S1: pzp to out
        *   S2: pzn to out
        *   S3: 0 to pzp
        *   S4: 0 to pzn
        *   But SYNC controllers are tied to the piezo current zero-crossings.
        *   S1/S3 would close at one peak, S2/S4 at the other.
        *   This is possible!
        *   Sync G1: edges="pos", closes S1 and S3.
        *   Sync G2: edges="neg", closes S2 and S4.
        *   This replaces the diodes with $2\Omega$ resistors. This should drastically improve $V_{avg}$ for S2 and S4.

    *   S1: pzp -> out (G1, pos)
    *   S2: pzn -> out (G2, neg)
    *   S3: 0 -> pzp (G1, pos)
    *   S4: 0 -> pzn (G2, neg)
    *   Is this correct?
        *   At positive peak of $V_{pzp}$ (current is zero), we want to move charge from $C_p$ to $C_{out}$.
        *   Actually, the current $I_p$ is $\sin(\omega t)$. The voltage $V_{pzp}$ is $-\cos(\omega t)$.
        *   The peaks of $V_{pzp}$ occur at $I_p = 0$ (zero crossings).
        *   At the positive peak of $V_{pzp}$, we want to connect pzp to out and pzn to 0.
        *   At the negative peak of $V_{pzp}$, we want to connect pzn to out and pzp to 0.
        *   This is exactly what G1 (pos) and G2 (neg) would do.
        *   Wait, the SYNC closes for a very short $t_{on}$. This isn't a continuous rectifier; it's a switched-capacitor converter.
        *   If $t_{on}$ is very short, we only transfer a small amount of charge. We need a larger $t_{on}$ or a different approach.
        *   Actually, the "Synchronous Electric Charge Extraction" (SECE) is exactly this. It uses an inductor to transfer the charge.
        *   SECE: $C_p$ is connected to $L$, and $L$ is connected to $C_{out}$ via a switch.
        *   Let's try: $pzp \to S1 \to L1 \to out$.
        *   At the positive peak of $V_{pzp}$, $S1$ closes, $L1$ transfers charge from $C_p$ to $C_{out}$.
        *   To do this for both halves:
            *   $pzp \to S1 \to L1 \to out$ (S1: G1, pos)
            *   $pzn \to S2 \to L1 \to out$ (S2: G2, neg)
            *   Wait, if $pzn$ is negative, $pzn \to L1 \to out$ will move charge *out* of $C_{out}$ unless there is a diode.
            *   Correct SECE:
                *   $pzp \to S1 \to n1$
                *   $pzn \to S2 \to n1$
                *   $n1 \to L1 \to D1 \to out$
                *   G1 (pos): closes S1.
                *   G2 (neg): closes S2.
                *   This transfers $C_p$ energy to $C_{out}$ at both peaks.

    *   **Design 1: SECE (Synchronous Electric Charge Extraction)**
        *   S1: [pzp, n1], ctrl: G1 (pos)
        *   S2: [pzn, n1], ctrl: G2 (neg)
        *   L1: [n1, n2]
        *   D1: [n2, out] (DSCH)
        *   Cout: [out, 0]
        *   Zener: [0, out] (DZ33)
        *   This should be very efficient (low drop).

    *   **Design 2: SSHI + FBR (Voltage multiplier)**
        *   L1: [pzp, n1]
        *   S1: [n1, pzn], ctrl: G1 (both)
        *   D1: [pzp, out], D2: [pzn, out], D3: [0, pzp], D4: [0, pzn] (FBR)
        *   Cout: [out, 0]
        *   Zener: [0, out] (DZ33)
        *   This increases the voltage before the FBR.

    *   **Design 3: Synchronous Bridge (Low-drop)**
        *   S1: [pzp, out], ctrl: G1 (pos)
        *   S2: [pzn, out], ctrl: G2 (neg)
        *   S3: [0, pzp], ctrl: G1 (pos)
        *   S4: [0, pzn], ctrl: G2 (neg)
        *   Cout: [out, 0]
        *   Zener: [0, out] (DZ33)
        *   (This is a switched-capacitor converter. Let's check if it can provide enough charge).
        *   Wait, $C_p$ is only 25nF. To get $V_{avg} = 2\text{V}$ with $R_L = 150\text{k}\Omega$ ($I_{load} = 13\mu\text{A}$), at $100\text{Hz}$, we need to move $13\mu\text{A} / 100\text{Hz} = 130\text{nC}$ per cycle.
        *   $Q = C_p \times \Delta V = 25\text{nF} \times 3.2\text{V} \approx 80\text{nC}$.
        *   Wait, the total charge per cycle from the piezo is $I_p / (2\pi f) = 50\mu\text{A} / (2\pi \times 100) \approx 80\text{nC}$.
        *   So the synchronous bridge *might* be enough, but the $t_{on}$ must be long enough to transfer the charge.

    *   *Re-evaluating Design 1 (SECE):*
        *   $pzp \to S1 \to n1$, $pzn \to S2 \to n1$, $n1 \to L1 \to D1 \to out$.
        *   At the positive peak, $S1$ closes. $L1$ and $C_p$ form a resonant circuit.
        *   The energy $1/2 C_p V_{peak}^2$ is transferred to $L1$ and then to $C_{out}$.
        *   This is very efficient.

    *   *Comparing SECE vs SSHI+FBR:*
        *   SECE is generally more efficient because it avoids the bridge's diode drops.
        *   SSHI+FBR increases the voltage, but still has the 2-diode drop.

    *   *Let's refine the SECE (Design 1):*
        *   L1 should be chosen such that $t_{on} \approx \pi \sqrt{L C_p}$.
        *   For $L=10\text{mH}, C_p=25\text{nF}, t_{on} \approx \pi \sqrt{10^{-2} \times 25 \times 10^{-9}} \approx 15\mu\text{s}$. This fits in the $t_{on}$ range ($1\mu\text{s}$ to $1\text{ms}$).
        *   S1: [pzp, n1], ctrl: G1, edges: pos
        *   S2: [pzn, n1], ctrl: G2, edges: neg
        *   L1: [n1, n2]
        *   D1: [n2, out], model: DSCH
        *   Cout: [out, 0]
        *   DZ1: [0, out], model: DZ33 (zener)

    *   *Let's refine the SSHI+FBR (Design 2):*
        *   L1: [pzp, n1], S1: [n1, pzn], ctrl: G1, edges: both
        *   FBR: D1[pzp, out], D2[pzn, out], D3[0, pzp], D4[0, pzn]
        *   Cout: [out, 0]
        *   DZ1: [0, out], model: DZ33

    *   *Let's try a third one: Modified FBR with a Boost Inductor (Design 3)*
        *   A simple way to boost $V_{avg}$ is to put an inductor in series with the rectifier.
        *   L1: [pzp, n1], D1: [n1, out], D2: [n1, pzn]... No.
        *   Let's try a different approach: A "Charge-Pump" using the SYNC.
        *   S1: [pzp, n1], ctrl: G1, edges: pos
        *   D1: [n1, out]
        *   S2: [pzn, n1], ctrl: G2, edges: neg
        *   D2: [n1, out]
        *   This is just a switched-capacitor pump. Without an inductor, it only moves $C_p \Delta V$.
        *   Wait, if we add a capacitor $C_{pump}$ at $n1$, we can move more charge.
        *   Let's stick to the SECE and SSHI. For the third, maybe a Half-Bridge with a Zener.

    *   *Wait, I have a better idea for Design 3: Parallel-SSHI.*
        *   Actually, the FBR was almost there. What if we just use a better rectifier?
        *   Let's try the "Synchronous Bridge" again but with a twist.
        *   S1: [pzp, out], G1 (pos)
        *   S2: [pzn, out], G2 (neg)
        *   S3: [0, pzp], G1 (pos)
        *   S4: [0, pzn], G2 (neg)
        *   But we need to make sure $C_{out}$ doesn't discharge back into the piezo.
        *   Wait, if we add diodes in series with the switches?
        *   S1 is [pzp, out], but we add D1 [pzp, out]. Then it's just a bridge.
        *   What if we use the SYNC to control the bridge?
        *   S1: [pzp, out], G1 (pos)
        *   S2: [pzn, out], G2 (neg)
        *   D1: [0, pzp], D2: [0, pzn]
        *   This way, we replace the two "top" diodes with switches. This reduces the drop from 2 diodes to 1 diode (since the return path is still through D1/D2).

    *   *Let's refine Design 3 (Hybrid Bridge):*
        *   S1: [pzp, out], G1, pos
        *   S2: [pzn, out], G2, neg
        *   D1: [0, pzp], DSCH
        *   D2: [0, pzn], DSCH
        *   Cout: [out, 0]
        *   DZ1: [0, out], DZ33
        *   This reduces the drop to $0.25\text{V}$ (from $0.5\text{V}$), which might be enough to fix S2 and S4.

    *   **Structure 1: SECE**
        *   S1 [pzp, n1] (G1, pos)
        *   S2 [pzn, n1] (G2, neg)
        *   L1 [n1, n2]
        *   D1 [n2, out] (DSCH)
        *   Cout [out, 0]
        *   DZ1 [0, out] (DZ33)
        *   Rationale: High efficiency, transfers $C_p$ energy using an inductor, minimal diode drop.

    *   **Structure 2: SSHI + FBR**
        *   L1 [pzp, n1], S1 [n1, pzn] (G1, both)
        *   D1 [pzp, out], D2 [pzn, out], D3 [0, pzp], D4 [0, pzn] (DSCH)
        *   Cout [out, 0]
        *   DZ1 [0, out] (DZ33)
        *   Rationale: Increases $V_{oc}$ by flipping $C_p$ voltage, but still uses FBR for rectification.

    *   **Structure 3: Hybrid Bridge**
        *   S1 [pzp, out] (G1, pos)
        *   S2 [pzn, out] (G2, neg)
        *   D1 [0, pzp], D2 [0, pzn] (DSCH)
        *   Cout [out, 0]
        *   DZ1 [0, out] (DZ33)
        *   Rationale: Reduces the voltage drop of the bridge by replacing the high-side diodes with synchronous switches.

    *   *S1 (nominal)*: All should work.
    *   *S2 (heavy load)*: Hybrid Bridge and SECE should be better than FBR.
    *   *S3 (strong excitation)*: DZ33 Zener protects $V_{max}$ in all three.
    *   *S4 (weak excitation)*: SECE and Hybrid Bridge should be better.
    *   *S5 (low freq)*: Stability ($dV$) should be handled by a sufficiently large $C_{out}$.
    *   *S6 (hot)*: Should be fine.

    Wait, in Structure 1 (SECE), the SYNC controller for S1 (pos) and S2 (neg) will pulse. The inductor $L1$ will transfer charge. This is a well-known high-efficiency topology.

    One detail: The $t_{on}$ for SECE is typically $\pi \sqrt{L C_p}$. For $L=10\text{mH}$, $t_{on} \approx 15\mu\text{s}$.
    For SSHI, $t_{on}$ is also $\pi \sqrt{L C_p}$.

    Wait, in Structure 1, if I have two switches S1, S2 and one inductor L1, and they both connect to $n1$, and $L1$ connects from $n1$ to $n2$, it works.

    *Self-Correction on Structure 3 (Hybrid Bridge):*
    S1 connects `pzp` to `out` at the positive peak.
    S2 connects `pzn` to `out` at the negative peak.
    If $V_{pzp}$ is positive and we connect it to `out`, and $V_{pzn}$ is negative and we connect it to `out`...
    Wait, $V_{pzn}$ is relative to `pzp`. If $pzp$ is at 3V and $pzn$ is at 0V, we connect $pzp \to out$. If $pzp$ is at 0V and $pzn$ is at 3V, we connect $pzn \to out$.
    But the piezo model is $Ip \sin(\omega t)$ in parallel with $C_p$. This means $V_{pzp} - V_{pzn}$ is the voltage.
    If $pzn$ is ground (0V), then $V_{pzp}$ is the voltage.
    If $pzn$ is not ground, the bridge handles it.
    In my Hybrid Bridge:
    $pzp \xrightarrow{S1} out$, $0 \xrightarrow{D1} pzp$ (during positive peak)
    $pzn \xrightarrow{S2} out$, $0 \xrightarrow{D2} pzn$ (during negative peak)
    This is exactly a bridge where the top diodes are replaced by switches.

    L1: 10mH (initial value)

    Ton: 15us (initial value)

    *   L-Cp inversion, ton is about $\pi \sqrt{L C_p}$.

    *   If $L = 10\text{mH}$, $t_{on} = \pi \sqrt{10^{-2} \times 25 \times 10^{-9}} \approx 15.7\mu\text{s}$.
    *   If $L = 1\text{mH}$, $t_{on} = \pi \sqrt{10^{-3} \times 25 \times 10^{-9}} \approx 5\mu\text{s}$.

    The `ton` will be optimized by the system, but I'll provide reasonable defaults.

    $L1$ is in series with $S1$ across the piezo.
    So $pzp \to L1 \to n1 \to S1 \to pzn$.
    This flips the voltage on $C_p$.
